modules.title: Program Design
modules.summary: Welcome to the Technical Program Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: Program Design. Program design is the TPM's core artifact: turning an ambiguous mandate into scope, milestones, dependencies, risks, and a communication plan that survives contact with four teams and two time zones. By the end of this module you will be able to scope an ambiguous initiative on the fly, map milestones and dependencies explicitly, define success criteria with real exit conditions, and walk an interviewer through a program brief the way the case rounds score it.
objectives: Understand and apply: scoping ambiguous initiatives
Understand and apply: milestones and dependency mapping
Understand and apply: defining success criteria and exit conditions
Understand and apply: risk registers and mitigation plans
Understand and apply: stakeholder mapping

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Program design** — The TPM's core artifact: turning an ambiguous mandate into scope, milestones, dependency maps, risks, and a communication plan.
- **Scoping ambiguous initiatives** — Drawing the boundary of a program: what is in, what is out, and what is explicitly deferred — before execution starts.
- **Milestones** — Named, dated, verifiable waypoints on the path to the program outcome; the skeleton the schedule hangs on.
- **Dependency mapping** — Making cross-team commitments explicit, owned, and sequenced — hidden dependencies are where programs die.
- **Success criteria** — The measurable definition of done; without them, "launch" is a matter of opinion.
- **Exit conditions** — The conditions under which the program stops: done, de-scoped, or cancelled — preventing zombie programs that never end.
- **Risk register** — The program's risk ledger: each risk with likelihood, impact, mitigation, and an owner — reviewed on a cadence, not filed away.
- **Stakeholder mapping** — Knowing who is impacted, who decides, and who needs informing — drawn before the program needs them.
- **Communication cadence** — The rhythm of information flow: right information to right stakeholders at the right tempo — preventing both surprise escalations and meeting sprawl.
- **Launch readiness** — The checklist proving the program can ship: owners, rollback, comms, and support — readiness verified, not assumed.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the 45-minute program-design interview rep. Set a timer — the case rounds are scored under pressure, so rehearse under pressure.
1. Take a blank page and write the ambiguous mandate at the top in one sentence — e.g. "Ship a new checkout flow across four teams in one quarter."
2. Scope it aloud: name three things in scope, two things explicitly out, and one thing deferred — ambiguity resolved on paper first.
3. List five milestones with verifiable done-states — "API contract frozen" not "API work done."
4. Draw the dependency map: every arrow is a cross-team commitment with an owner; circle the two you would worry about most and say why.
5. Write the success criteria with exit conditions: the metric that says "done," and the condition that would stop the program.
6. Fill a risk register: three risks, each with likelihood, impact, a mitigation, and an owner.
7. Design the communication cadence: who gets what, on what rhythm — the escalation path for when a dependency slips.
8. Close by reading back the one-page program brief: problem, scope, milestones, risks, asks — in under two minutes, as you would to the interviewer.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your interview prep brief: produce the one-page program brief for a cross-team launch and defend it in a 45-minute case rep.
The scenario. You are the TPM for a new checkout flow that touches the storefront team, payments team, fraud team, and data platform team, with two of the four teams in different time zones. Launch is one quarter out and the mandate is still ambiguous.
Deliverables.
- A one-page program brief: problem, scope (in/out/deferred), five milestones with verifiable done-states, a dependency map with owners, success criteria with exit conditions, a risk register (likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner), and a communication cadence with escalation paths.
- A two-minute verbal walkthrough of the brief as you would deliver it in the case round.
Grading lens. The interviewer scores structured thinking, not the right answer: did ambiguity shrink on paper, are dependencies owned, are exit conditions real, and did the verbal walkthrough land the structure without rambling? Time yourself; the round is 45 minutes.

modules.title: Execution Engine
modules.summary: Welcome back to the TPM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Execution Engine. Program design gets the artifact on paper; execution is where programs are won or lost: the status discipline, dependency hygiene, and escalation judgment that keep a multi-team plan moving when reality diverges from the Gantt chart. By the end of this module you will run status reporting that drives decisions, manage cross-team dependencies proactively, unblock as a daily craft, escalate deliberately, and run retrospectives that actually change behavior.
objectives: Understand and apply: status reporting that drives decisions
Understand and apply: dependency management across teams
Understand and apply: unblocking: the TPM's daily craft
Understand and apply: escalation paths and when to use them
Understand and apply: tradeoff triage under schedule pressure

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Execution** — The daily craft of keeping a multi-team program moving: status discipline, dependency hygiene, unblocking, and escalation judgment.
- **Decision-driving status** — Status reporting built around risks, asks, and options — not activity lists. Status exists to move decisions forward.
- **Dependency management** — Tracking cross-team commitments, spotting slips early, and renegotiating before the slip becomes a miss.
- **Unblocking** — The TPM's highest-frequency value: finding who can make the stuck decision and getting it made.
- **Escalation path** — A deliberate route for decisions that exceed your authority or stalls that exceed their budget — used deliberately, with options attached.
- **Tradeoff triage** — Making the cost explicit under schedule pressure: scope, date, or quality — decided by whoever owns the outcome.
- **Multi-quarter planning** — Keeping a long plan on rails: rolling milestones, dependency re-checks, and honest re-plans when reality diverges.
- **Blameless retrospective** — The post-cycle review that changes behavior: blameless analysis plus action items with owners and due dates, revisited — otherwise theater.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the one-week execution cadence drill on a simulated program. Use a real or invented multi-team plan — the mechanics are the craft.
1. Write the week's one-page status: three risks, two asks, and the options behind each — no activity lists allowed.
2. Walk the dependency map and mark every commitment due this week; email or message (write the actual message) the owner of any at-risk commitment to renegotiate before it slips.
3. List everything stuck right now and identify the decision each item is waiting on; for the top item, name the decision-maker and write the exact question you will ask them today.
4. Take one stalled item and decide deliberately whether to escalate: does the decision exceed your authority, or has the stall exceeded its budget? If yes, write the escalation with options attached.
5. Run a tradeoff triage: pick a schedule-pressure item and make scope/date/quality explicit in writing; name the outcome owner who must decide.
6. At the end of the week, run a 30-minute retrospective: blameless timeline, two action items with owners and due dates — and schedule the revisit of those actions.
7. Debrief aloud in five minutes: what moved this week because of your execution craft, and what did you learn about your own escalation timing?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your interview prep brief: demonstrate execution craft on a program where reality has diverged from the plan.
The scenario. Mid-quarter, three of your eight teams report slips: a dependency the fraud team owed payments is two weeks late, the data platform API contract changed without notice, and the executive sponsor is asking whether the launch date holds.
Deliverables.

- A dependency triage: which commitments are at risk, what you renegotiated, and with whom.
- A written escalation for the one decision you cannot make yourself — with options attached.
- A tradeoff recommendation for the launch date: scope/date/quality made explicit, outcome owner named.
- A retrospective plan: the blameless questions you would ask the team after the launch, and two action items with owners and dates.
Grading lens. Behavioral rounds score judgment, not luck: did you surface problems early, escalate deliberately with options, and show a retrospective habit that changes behavior?

modules.title: Cross-Functional Leadership
modules.summary: Welcome back to the TPM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 3: Cross-Functional Leadership. TPMs own outcomes they cannot command. This module teaches the influence toolkit: stakeholder maps, decision logs, crisp escalations, and the follow-through that makes teams trust your coordination. By the end of this module you will align engineering managers and PMs on shared outcomes, resolve cross-team conflict with the tradeoff explicit, write executive pre-reads that respect executive time, and drive decisions in ambiguous ownership.
objectives: Understand and apply: influence without authority
Understand and apply: aligning engineering managers and PMs
Understand and apply: conflict resolution between teams
Understand and apply: executive communication and pre-reads
Understand and apply: driving decisions in ambiguous ownership

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Influence without authority** — The TPM's core currency: stakeholder maps, decision logs, crisp escalations, and relentless follow-through — trust compounded over time.
- **Connective tissue** — The TPM's organizational role: carrying context across team boundaries so multi-team programs stay coherent.
- **Decision log** — The written record of who decided what, when, and why — ambiguity dies where decisions are logged.
- **Alignment** — A document before it is a feeling: shared outcomes, explicit tradeoffs, and written agreements between engineering managers and PMs.
- **Conflict resolution** — Reframing around the shared goal, surfacing the real constraint, deciding with the tradeoff explicit — then recording it.
- **Executive communication** — Pre-reads carrying the decision needed, the options, and the recommendation — respect for executive time earns executive trust.
- **Ambiguous ownership** — Resolved when someone names the decision, proposes the owner, and sets the deadline — ambiguity hates documentation.
- **Trust across organizations** — Built by follow-through on coordination promises: what you said would happen, happened.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the cross-functional influence drill. Pick a real or simulated two-team dispute or ambiguous decision — the mechanics work on any material.
1. Draw the stakeholder map: who is impacted, who decides, who needs informing — for both teams.
2. Write the decision log entry: name the decision, propose the owner, set the deadline — write it down even if it feels premature.
3. Draft a one-page alignment document: the shared outcome, the explicit tradeoffs, and the written agreement both sides will sign off on.
4. If there is conflict, reframe it in writing around the shared goal: surface the real constraint (capacity? priority? information?) and record the decision with its tradeoff.
5. Write the executive pre-read for the decision: the decision needed, the options, your recommendation — one page, respectful of executive time.
6. Follow through: send the updates you promised on the rhythm you promised — and log that you did.
7. Debrief aloud in three minutes: where did influence work, where did it stall, and which tool (map, log, pre-read, follow-through) moved it?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your interview prep brief: show influence without authority on a conflict between two teams.
The scenario. The payments team and the fraud team disagree on the checkout program's fraud-review scope: payments wants speed, fraud wants rigor, and both report to different VPs. The launch date is held by the executive sponsor, who wants a recommendation this week.
Deliverables.
- A stakeholder map and a decision log entry with the decision named, owner proposed, deadline set.
- A one-page alignment document both teams can sign: shared outcome, explicit tradeoffs, written agreements.
- An executive pre-read: decision needed, options, your recommendation — one page.
- A three-minute spoken walkthrough of how you influenced the outcome without owning either team.
Grading lens. Cross-functional rounds score process, not authority: did you reframe around the shared outcome, surface the real constraint, record the decision — and earn trust through follow-through?

modules.title: Technical Depth for TPMs
modules.summary: Welcome back to the TPM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 4: Technical Depth for TPMs. TPM interviews probe technical depth without requiring you to code. This module builds the literacy to read designs, question tradeoffs, and spot integration risk — and the humility to know where your depth ends. By the end of this module you will read architecture documents critically, reason about API contracts and integration points, speak SLOs and error budgets fluently, and ask the sharp technical questions that show you understand the tradeoff space.
objectives: Understand and apply: system design literacy for non-coders
Understand and apply: reading architecture documents critically
Understand and apply: API contracts and integration points
Understand and apply: data pipelines: sources, transforms, sinks
Understand and apply: reliability and SLO literacy

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Technical depth for TPMs** — Literacy, not coding: reading designs critically, spotting integration risk, and questioning tradeoffs — plus the humility to know where your depth ends.
- **System-design literacy (non-coder)** — Reading architecture docs for components, data flow, and failure modes — enough to question tradeoffs intelligently.
- **Critical reading of architecture docs** — Asking what breaks, what scales, what was decided and why — the questions that reveal the design's real risks.
- **API contracts and integration points** — The boundaries where systems meet: schemas, versions, error handling — where integration risk lives.
- **Data pipelines** — Sources, transforms, sinks — and where data quality or latency breaks downstream promises.
- **SLO literacy** — SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets: what "reliable enough" costs — the language of production commitments.
- **Sharp technical questions** — Probes of assumptions, alternatives considered, and failure modes — questions that show you understand the tradeoff space.
- **Deferral with humility** — Knowing when to defer to engineering judgment on implementation choices within agreed constraints — humility that builds engineering trust.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the technical-depth rep on a real architecture document — from your own past work if you have one, or a public design doc you can reference.
1. Read the document once and sketch its component diagram: components, data flow, and the integration points between systems.
2. Mark every API contract and integration point with a red flag — these are where integration risk lives.
3. Trace one end-to-end data pipeline through the diagram: source, transform, sink — and write down where data quality or latency could break a downstream promise.
4. Ask the three critical questions in writing: what breaks first, what scales worst, and what was decided and why.
5. Write the SLO question: what is the production commitment here, what does "reliable enough" cost, and where is the error budget?
6. Draft three sharp technical questions you would ask the design's author — each probing an assumption, an alternative, or a failure mode.
7. Mark in writing the boundary of your own depth: which judgments you can defend, and which you would defer to engineering judgment — humility on paper.
8. Present the whole reading aloud in ten minutes: the design, its risks, your questions, and your deferral boundary.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your interview prep brief: prove technical depth without writing code.
The scenario. Your TPM technical round hands you a design doc for a notification pipeline: an API ingests events, a queue buffers them, workers render templates, and an email/SMS provider delivers. The interviewer asks you to find the risks.
Deliverables.
- A component-and-data-flow sketch with integration points flagged.
- A written critical reading: what breaks first, what scales worst, what was decided and why.
- The SLO reading: the production commitment, the error-budget implication, the "reliable enough" cost.
- Three sharp technical questions probing assumptions, alternatives, and failure modes.
- A stated deferral boundary: what you can defend, and what you would hand to engineering judgment.
Grading lens. The round scores literacy plus judgment, with humility: did you find the real integration risks, speak the reliability language, ask questions that reveal the tradeoff space — and know where your depth ends?

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Program case** — The TPM case round's unit of work: a program scenario you structure aloud — scope, milestones, dependencies, risks, comms — narrated live.

- **Turnaround case** — The failing-program scenario: diagnose first (red signals, unowned dependencies, unclear exit), then re-scope, re-plan, and re-communicate with owners named.
- **Platform-migration case** — Treated as a program, not a deploy: hard dependencies sequenced, rollback planned, consumers migrated with support.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the three-case circuit. Work each case aloud with a timer — 30 minutes per case — and write the one-pager after.

6. Read a real incident postmortem (public ones are fine) as a TPM: extract the timeline, the action items with owners, and judge whether the follow-through happened.
7. Write the one-page program brief for the launch case: problem, scope, milestones, risks, asks — one page, no overflow.
8. Review each case aloud in two minutes: what structure did you show, where did you ramble, what would you change?

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **TPM loop** — The standard onsite circuit: program design, technical depth, and behavioral rounds — the full circuit, timed.
- **Program deep-dive stories** — Two or three programs told with structure: ambiguity faced, design produced, execution challenges, outcome, learning.
- **Technical round (TPM)** — Probes design literacy and tradeoff questioning — not coding, but genuine technical judgment.
- **TPM behavioral stories** — The role's greatest hits: influence without authority, conflict resolution, failed programs, stakeholder wins.
- **Mock structure and timing** — Realistic conditions per round with a clock — pressure practiced, not first felt on the day.
- **Self-review rubrics** — Scoring your own answers against the round's bar — turning each mock into a sharper next attempt.
- **Iteration between mocks** — Feedback that changes the next round; mocks without iteration are anxiety rehearsal.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the full TPM mock circuit. Schedule three back-to-back sessions with a partner or record yourself; real clocks, real conditions.
1. Mock 1 — program design (45 min): given an ambiguous mandate, scope, milestone, map, and risk aloud while the clock runs; no pausing.
2. Immediately self-review with the rubric: structure audible? dependencies owned? exit conditions real? Score yourself honestly.
3. Mock 2 — technical depth (30 min): your partner hands you a design doc or system description; read it critically, flag integration risks, and ask your sharp questions aloud.
4. Self-review: did you find the real risks, speak SLOs, ask tradeoff questions — and mark your deferral boundary honestly?
5. Mock 3 — behavioral (30 min): tell two deep-dive stories (ambiguity faced, design, execution, outcome, learning) and one influence-without-authority story; your partner asks follow-ups.
6. Self-review: tight structure? your role explicit? real learning named? Score against the bar.
7. Write the iteration plan: the three specific changes you will make before the next circuit — mocks without iteration are anxiety rehearsal.
8. Run the circuit again in one week and measure the delta against this week's rubric scores.

modules.title: People Leadership
modules.summary: Welcome to the Engineering Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: People Leadership. The people half of the EM role: 1:1s, feedback, coaching, and the hard conversations — taught as skills with reps, not traits you either have or do not. By the end of this module you will run 1:1s that belong to the report, give feedback that lands, choose coaching over managing when the moment needs it, handle performance management fairly, and build psychological safety by how you react to bad news, daily.
objectives: Understand and apply: running effective 1:1s

Understand and apply: performance management and PIPs

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **1:1** — The report's meeting: their agenda, their growth, their blockers — the manager listens, coaches, and unblocks.
- **Feedback that lands** — Private, specific, behavioral, impact-linked — and timely; feedback delayed is feedback denied.
- **Coaching versus managing** — Coaching grows the person's own solutions; managing directs outcomes — know which the moment needs.
- **Performance management** — Done fairly: clear expectations, documented feedback, support offered, timelines, honest consequences — process before punishment.
- **PIP (performance improvement plan)** — The formal last step of fair performance management: documented expectations, support, and a timeline — never the first move.
- **Team conflict** — Handled early, privately, and on interests not positions — small conflicts addressed beat big ones mediated.
- **Psychological safety in practice** — People raising risks and mistakes without fear — built by how you react to bad news, daily.
- **Managing former peers** — Re-earning authority after promotion: clear expectations, no favoritism — name the changed relationship.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the people-leadership rep week. Use a real or simulated team member for each exercise — the mechanics work on either.
1. Hold a 1:1 using the report's agenda: open with their topics, listen more than you speak, and close with one unblocking action that is yours.
2. Write one piece of real feedback using the discipline: private, specific, behavioral, impact-linked — and note whether it was timely or delayed.
3. Take a coaching moment: ask three open questions before offering any directive — practice growing their solution instead of directing yours.
4. Write a fair performance-management sequence for an underperformer: clear expectations, documented feedback, support offered, timeline — process before punishment, PIP only if the pattern holds.
5. Rehearse a team-conflict conversation: early, private, on interests not positions — script your opening line and your close.
6. Audit your own psychological safety: recall the last piece of bad news you received — write down exactly how you reacted, and what the team learned from it.
7. Debrief aloud in five minutes: which mode did you default to — coaching or managing — and did the moment actually need it?

modules.title: Delivery Ownership
modules.summary: Welcome back to the EM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Delivery Ownership. Delivery is the EM's promise to the business: planning with honest estimates, owning incidents, and the upward communication that keeps trust when dates move. By the end of this module you will plan sprints and quarters with capacity-awareness, estimate with ranges and stated assumptions, own roadmap accountability, run a blameless incident culture, manage up on delivery risk with no surprises, and say no to protect the team.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Delivery ownership** — The EM's promise to the business: commitments made carefully, communicated honestly, kept visibly.
- **Sprint and quarterly planning** — Capacity-aware, assumption-explicit, buffer-honest — plans that survive contact with reality.
- **Estimation without fantasy** — Ranges plus stated assumptions, calibrated by history — single-point dates are wishes.
- **Roadmap accountability** — Owning the outcomes the roadmap promised — and saying early when reality diverges.
- **Incident ownership** — The EM sets the culture: blameless, learning-driven, action items with owners — incidents are inevitable, repeats are choices.
- **On-call culture** — The human side of incidents: sustainable rotations, respected pages, and the learning loop that keeps the pager quiet.
- **Managing up on delivery risk** — Early, with options: the risk, its impact, the mitigations, the ask — surprises destroy trust, updates build it.
- **Saying no** — Protecting focus and sustainable pace: no with a rationale is a strategy; no without one is just obstruction.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the delivery-ownership drill on your next real (or simulated) sprint. Work it end to end — planning to retrospective.
1. Write the sprint plan capacity-aware: list actual available capacity, name the assumptions, and add an honest buffer — no fantasy numbers.
2. Estimate the three biggest items as ranges with stated assumptions: best/likely/worst, and what you would need to believe for each.
3. Pick one roadmap commitment and write the accountability statement: what outcome was promised, what the current trajectory shows, and when you would say something if they diverge.
4. Draft the delivery-risk update for your manager: the risk, its impact, the mitigations, the ask — early and with options, no surprises.
5. Rehearse saying no to one plausible request: no, because [strategy/capacity tradeoff], and here is what the team is doing instead.
6. Write the incident-culture memo: blameless, learning-driven, action items with owners — what repeats are choices your team refuses to make.
7. Debrief aloud in five minutes: where did honesty about capacity change a decision, and where did a surprise almost happen?

- A "no" with rationale for the new request that just arrived: what the team stops or delays to protect focus.
- An incident-culture statement for the team: blameless, learning-driven, owned action items.

modules.title: Hiring and Growing Teams
modules.summary: Welcome back to the EM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 3: Hiring and Growing Teams. Teams are built, not found. From loop design to calibration to retention, this module treats hiring and growth as the EM's highest-leverage system. By the end of this module you will set and hold the hiring bar, design interview loops with signal per round, run structured interviews and honest debriefs, onboard for ramp speed, maintain career ladders and calibration, and retain the people you cannot lose.

Understand and apply: designing interview loops
Understand and apply: structured interviews and debriefs
Understand and apply: onboarding for ramp speed
Understand and apply: career ladders and leveling

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Hiring bar** — The EM's highest-leverage system: every hire compounds for years — the bar shapes the team more than any process.
- **Interview loop** — Designed, not ritual: signal per round, no redundancy, structured questions, trained interviewers.
- **Structured interviews** — Comparable signal across candidates: same questions, same rubric — fairness and comparability by design.
- **Debrief** — The hiring decision meeting: honest, evidence-based, and able to say no — debriefs that can reject protect the bar.
- **Onboarding for ramp speed** — 30/60/90 clarity, a buddy, early wins scoped — time-to-productivity designed, not hoped for.
- **Career ladders and leveling** — Transparent growth paths and consistent expectations — fairness made legible.
- **Calibration** — Comparing judgments across teams so "strong" means the same everywhere — equity in evaluation.
- **Retention** — Keeping the people you cannot lose: growth, recognition, and the work itself — managed deliberately, not discovered at the exit interview.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the hiring-system drill. Design the loop for a role you know well — real or simulated.
1. Write the hiring bar for the role: the three things a yes-candidate must demonstrate, in observable terms.
2. Design the loop: one round per distinct signal, no redundancy — name the signal each round owns.
3. Write the structured questions and the rubric for one round: same questions, same scoring, for every candidate.
4. Rehearse the debrief: present evidence for and against, and practice saying no with reasons — the debrief must be able to reject.
5. Draft the 30/60/90 onboarding plan: clarity per phase, a named buddy, and an early win scoped small enough to land in week one.
6. Write the retention check for your best engineer: growth path, recognition, the work itself — what would you change before the exit interview?
7. Debrief aloud in five minutes: where is your current loop weakest — signal, structure, or the courage to say no?

notes.body:

Grading lens. Hiring rounds score systems thinking: is there signal per round, can the debrief reject, is ramp speed designed — and is retention proactive?

modules.summary: Welcome back to the EM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 4: Engineering Strategy. Beyond the sprint: the strategy layer EM interviews probe — technical vision, debt strategy, and platform decisions tied to business outcomes, not just engineering taste. By the end of this module you will write a technical vision, quantify and fund tech debt as a portfolio, make deliberate build-versus-buy platform bets, read engineering health metrics, align engineering strategy with product strategy, and plan long-range without fiction.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Technical vision** — A 2–3 year picture of where the systems go and why — direction the team can build toward.
- **Tech debt (strategic)** — Quantify it, prioritize against features, fund paydown — debt as a managed portfolio, not a complaint.
- **Platform bets** — Build-versus-buy decisions: differentiating IP you build, commodity you buy — weighed with total cost of ownership and team skill, deliberately.
- **Engineering health metrics** — Deploy frequency, change failure rate, review latency, on-call burden — the system's vital signs.
- **Strategy alignment** — Every technical bet traces to a product outcome — architecture in service of the business, not taste.
- **Long-range planning without fiction** — Direction with explicit uncertainty: bets, hedges, and review points — honest about what is unknown.
- **Total cost of ownership (TCO)** — The full price of a platform decision: build cost, operate cost, migrate cost, and the attention cost — weighed deliberately, not just the sticker price.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the strategy drill. Pick a system you know — real or simulated — and produce the strategy layer.
1. Write the technical vision: a 2–3 year picture of where this system goes and why — one page, direction a team can build toward.
2. List the top five tech debts: quantify each (what it costs in velocity, incidents, or risk), prioritize against feature work, and propose the funding ask.
3. Take one platform decision and run build-versus-buy deliberately: differentiating IP versus commodity, total cost of ownership, team skill — with numbers, not vibes.
4. Define the engineering health metrics you would watch: deploy frequency, change failure rate, review latency, on-call burden — and the thresholds that would worry you.
5. Trace one technical bet to a product outcome in writing: if you cannot draw the line to the business, the bet is taste, not strategy.
6. Write the long-range plan with explicit uncertainty: the bets, the hedges, and the review points where you revisit — honest about what is unknown.
7. Present the strategy aloud in ten minutes: vision, debt portfolio, platform bet, health metrics — as you would to a VP.

modules.summary: Welcome back to the EM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 5: Guided Leadership Scenarios. Reps on the situations EM interviews are built from: underperformance, reorgs, missed dates, and disputes — practiced until your answers have structure under pressure. By the end of this module you will handle the underperforming senior, lead through a reorg you did not choose, surface a deadline miss with options, mediate a cross-team dispute, plan scaling from 5 to 15, lead through an incident, and debrief your own decisions.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Leadership scenario** — The EM interview's unit of work: a realistic situation you reason through aloud — structure under pressure.
- **Underperformer playbook** — Private, specific feedback with support offered — documented; escalation to formal process only if the pattern holds.
- **Reorg leadership** — Leading through a reorg you did not choose: translate it for the team honestly, protect what matters, execute the transition well — leadership in constraint.
- **Deadline-miss surfacing** — Surface early with options and tradeoffs — managing up beats the surprise; renegotiate scope, date, or quality explicitly.
- **Dispute mediation** — Interests over positions, shared outcome reframed, decision recorded — mediation with a paper trail.
- **Scaling 5→15** — What breaks: communication paths, onboarding, informal process — deliberately add structure before the chaos.
- **Incident leadership** — Command structure, comms cadence, blameless follow-through — calm is a leadership output.
- **Decision debrief** — Reviewing your own calls afterward: what you decided, what you missed, what you would change — the habit that compounds judgment.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the seven-scenario circuit. Work each scenario aloud with a timer — 10 minutes each — then debrief.
1. The underperforming senior: script your first move — private, specific feedback with support offered, documented — and where the line to formal process sits.
2. The reorg you did not choose: write the honest translation you would give the team, name what you will protect, and list the transition's three execution risks.
3. The deadline the team will miss: draft the early surfacing message — options and tradeoffs, scope/date/quality explicit — and rehearse delivering it.
4. The cross-team dispute: map interests versus positions for both sides, reframe the shared outcome, and write the recorded decision.
5. Scaling from 5 to 15: list what breaks — communication paths, onboarding, informal process — and the structure you would add before the chaos.
6. Leading through an incident: define the command structure, the comms cadence, and the blameless follow-through you would run.
7. Debrief each scenario aloud in two minutes: what structure did you show, where did you hesitate, what would you change?
8. Write one paragraph on your own hardest real leadership decision — the debrief habit starts with your own history.

Product sense is structured empathy: clarifying the user and the problem before any solution, prioritizing with stated assumptions, and critiquing products by mechanism rather than taste. By the end of this module you will show user empathy with specific humans, frame problems before solutions, ask 'why' honestly five times, read markets and competitors, prioritize with impact versus effort and stated assumptions, and structure open-ended product questions so the interviewer can follow your thinking.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Product sense** — Structured empathy: clarifying the user and the problem before any solution — sense before execution.
- **User empathy** — Naming who hurts, how often, and what they do today — specific humans, not personas-as-wallpaper.
- **Problem framing** — Framing the problem before solutions: solutions to the wrong problem are waste — the frame decides everything downstream.
- **Five whys (honest)** — Drilling past symptoms to the real need — honestly, not performatively.
- **Market and competitive understanding** — Knowing the landscape: who competes, how they differentiate, and where the opening is.

Execution rounds test whether you can ship: scoping with engineers, prioritizing under constraints, and turning launches into iteration loops instead of one-shot bets. notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Roadmapping under constraints** — Sequencing bets with honest capacity, dependencies, and uncertainty — the roadmap as a communication tool, not a promise.

- **Scoping with engineering** — Tradeoffs together: scope, date, quality — the PM brings the why, engineering brings the how, decisions are shared.
- **Launch readiness** — The checklist: owners, rollback, comms, support, monitoring — readiness verified before users arrive.
- **Post-launch iteration loops** — Measure, learn, iterate — launches are hypotheses with a plan, not one-shot bets.
- **Saying no (PM)** — No, because [strategy/metric tradeoff], and here is what we are doing instead — no without rationale is just obstruction.
- **Stakeholder management through delivery** — Keeping stakeholders aligned as reality moves: early flags, options, and the tradeoff made explicit.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the execution drill on a feature you know — real or simulated. Work the full ship cycle on paper.
1. Write the roadmap for the next quarter: sequence three bets with honest capacity, named dependencies, and the uncertainty stated — a communication tool, not a promise.
2. Run the everything-is-P0 triage: score the three bets on impact versus effort with assumptions stated, rank them, and write the tradeoff conversation you would have with stakeholders.
3. Scope one bet with engineering: write the scope/date/quality tradeoff as a shared decision — the PM's why, engineering's how, the decision recorded.
4. Build the launch checklist: owners, rollback, comms, support, monitoring — and mark each verified or not-yet; unverified items are launch blockers.
5. Design the post-launch iteration loop: the metrics you will watch, the hypotheses you will test, the cadence — the launch as a hypothesis with a plan.
6. Write a no with a rationale for one plausible request: the strategy or metric tradeoff, and what you are doing instead.
7. Draft the stakeholder update for a two-week slip: early, with options, the tradeoff explicit — managing stakeholders through delivery.
8. Debrief aloud in five minutes: where did constraint change a decision, and where did the loop replace a one-shot bet?

modules.title: Metrics and Judgment
modules.summary: Welcome back to the PM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Metrics and Judgment. Metrics separate PMs who guess from PMs who learn: defining measures that track user value, reading experiments honestly, and debugging moves before reacting to them. By the end of this module you will define success metrics tied to user value, read funnels and cohorts fluently, design A/B tests with significance discipline, debug a moved metric before reacting, estimate sanely, make judgment calls with incomplete data, and spot the failure modes of north-star metrics.
objectives: Understand and apply: defining success metrics tied to user value
Understand and apply: analytics literacy: funnels, cohorts, retention
Understand and apply: A/B testing: design, significance, and pitfalls
Understand and apply: debugging a metric that moved
Understand and apply: estimation questions done sanely

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Success metric** — Tied to user value, measurable, with known failure modes — metrics that track learning, not vanity.
- **Analytics literacy (PM)** — Funnels, cohorts, retention — reading the product's vital signs without waiting for an analyst.
- **Funnel** — The step-by-step conversion path: where users drop is where the product leaks.
- **Cohort analysis** — Behavior compared by group and over time — the diagnostic pair with funnels.
- **A/B testing** — Design upfront, pre-registered metrics, significance discipline, and pitfall awareness: peeking, novelty effects, unexamined segments.
- **Metric debugging** — Instrumentation, segments, confounders, external events — understand the move before reacting to it.
- **Estimation (sane)** — State assumptions, round-number math, sanity-check the answer — the reasoning chain is the grade.
- **Judgment with incomplete data** — Decide reversibly fast, irreversibly carefully — and name what would change your mind.
- **North-star metric** — The one metric that best captures user value delivered — with known failure modes and counter-metrics.
- **Goodhart's law** — When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — the north star's failure mode, guarded with counter-metrics.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the metrics-and-judgment rep set. Work each rep on paper — the reasoning chain is the grade.
1. Define a success metric for a feature you know: tie it to user value, make it measurable, and name its failure modes — vanity check included.
2. Read a funnel: sketch signup-to-value for a product you use, mark where users drop, and write the one question each drop raises.
3. Compare two cohorts in writing: new versus returning users on one behavior — what differs, and what would you test next?
4. Design an A/B test: the hypothesis, the pre-registered primary metric, the sample-size thinking, and the pitfalls you will guard (peeking, novelty, segments).
5. Debug a moved metric: pick a metric that could move, and walk instrumentation → segments → confounders → external events before writing any reaction.
6. Do a guesstimate sanely: state assumptions, do round-number math, sanity-check the answer — the chain matters more than the number.
7. Make a judgment call with incomplete data: decide one reversible thing fast and one irreversible thing carefully — and write what would change your mind.
8. Pick a north-star candidate and name its Goodhart failure mode plus the counter-metric that guards it.

modules.summary: Welcome back to the PM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 6: PM Mock Circuit. The full circuit, simulated: sense, execution, metrics, and behavioral rounds under real timing, with rubrics and recording review that make each mock sharper than the last. notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **PM loop** — Sense, execution, metrics, behavioral — the full circuit under real timing.
- **Full-loop simulation** — Back-to-back rounds with clocks — stamina and transitions practiced, not just content.
- **Timing discipline** — Knowing each round's shape and budget — where to spend minutes, when to land the plane.
- **Rubric scoring (product)** — Structure, user focus, tradeoff awareness, data grounding — the dimensions interviewers actually grade.
- **Recording review** — You hear the rambling you cannot feel — recordings make "tight" measurable.
- **Iteration between mocks** — Targeted fixes re-tested under pressure — each mock sharper than the last by design.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the full PM mock loop. Schedule four back-to-back rounds with a partner or record yourself; real clocks.
1. Round 1 — product sense (30 min): a design question and a teardown — structure audible, user first, assumptions stated.
2. Round 2 — execution (30 min): roadmap and prioritization under P0 pressure — ship judgment, tradeoffs explicit.
3. Round 3 — metrics (30 min): a moved metric debugged live plus a guesstimate — reasoning chains, not numbers.
4. Round 4 — behavioral (30 min): two stories in tight STAR plus your interviewer questions — preparation and honesty.
5. Rubric-score every round immediately: structure, user focus, tradeoff awareness, data grounding — score honestly.
6. Review the recordings: mark every ramble, every unstated assumption, every landed plane — make "tight" measurable.
7. Write the iteration plan: three targeted fixes for the next loop — each mock sharper than the last by design.
8. Run the loop again in one week and measure the delta on the rubric dimensions.

modules.title: Technical Depth for PMs
modules.summary: Welcome to the Technical Product Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: Technical Depth for PMs. Enough engineering to be dangerous in the good way: how systems are built, where they break, and how to reason about scale — the depth technical PM interviews actually test. By the end of this module you will reason about the web at PM altitude, compare databases by access pattern, weigh caching's speed against staleness, use queues for async scale, read technical docs for commitments, and estimate scale with sane round-number math.
objectives: Understand and apply: how the web works: requests, responses, latency
Understand and apply: databases: relational versus document
Understand and apply: caching: what it buys and what it risks
Understand and apply: queues and async processing
Understand and apply: system design literacy for PMs

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **The web at PM altitude** — Requests and responses over HTTP; latency from network + compute + data — enough to reason about performance tradeoffs.
- **Relational versus document databases** — Relational: structured, joins, strong consistency. Document: flexible schema, nested data, scale-out — match to the access pattern.
- **Caching** — What it buys: speed — fewer origin hits, lower latency. What it risks: staleness — invalidation strategy is the real design work.
- **Queues and async processing** — Decoupling slow work from the request path — reliability and scale via buffering and retries.
- **System-design literacy (PM)** — Components, data flow, bottlenecks, failure modes — enough to connect architecture choices to user outcomes and cost.
- **Reading technical docs and RFCs** — Reading for decisions and contracts: what is promised, what is assumed, what can change — the PM reads for commitments.
- **Scale estimation** — Users → requests per second → storage → bandwidth, assumptions stated — round-number math, sanity-checked.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the technical-depth rep set. Work each rep on paper — reasoning, not trivia.
1. Trace a web request at PM altitude: browser → DNS → load balancer → app → database — and name where latency comes from at each hop.
2. Compare databases for a real product you know: write the access pattern, then choose relational or document — and justify the choice by the pattern, not by fashion.
3. Weigh a caching decision: what it buys (speed, fewer origin hits) against what it risks (staleness) — and write the invalidation strategy, which is the real design work.
4. Design an async path: pick a slow operation and decouple it with a queue — buffering, retries, and what happens when the queue backs up.
5. Read a technical doc or RFC section for commitments: what is promised, what is assumed, what can change — write the three lists.
6. Estimate scale sanely: users → requests per second → storage → bandwidth, assumptions stated, round numbers — then sanity-check the answer.
7. Present one rep aloud in five minutes: the tradeoff you weighed and the reasoning chain — the PM's technical performance.

modules.title: API and Platform Thinking
modules.summary: Welcome back to the Technical PM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: API and Platform Thinking. APIs are products with developer customers. This module covers design tradeoffs, versioning discipline, and the unglamorous contract work that decides whether a platform gets adopted. By the end of this module you will discuss REST tradeoffs credibly, weigh versioning as a compatibility promise, choose between webhooks and polling deliberately, think in platforms versus products, and treat developer experience as the product.
objectives: Understand and apply: REST literacy: resources, methods, status codes
Understand and apply: API design tradeoffs
Understand and apply: versioning and compatibility promises
Understand and apply: webhooks versus polling
Understand and apply: platform versus product: different customers

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **REST literacy** — Resources, methods, status codes — the vocabulary for discussing API design tradeoffs credibly.
- **API design tradeoffs** — Granularity, consistency, evolvability — each choice taxes some consumers to benefit others; name who pays.
- **Versioning** — Compatibility promises that let developers build without fear — versioning discipline decides platform adoption.
- **Webhooks versus polling** — Webhooks: push, real-time, needs receiver infra. Polling: pull, simple, wasteful — match to latency needs and consumer capability.
- **Platform versus product** — Different customers: platform customers are developers — their product is your API's developer experience. Different users, different success metrics.
- **Developer experience (DX)** — Docs, SDKs, errors, onboarding — the DX is the UI of a platform; it decides adoption.
- **Rate limits, auth, and the boring parts** — The unglamorous contract work: auth, limits, idempotency, deprecation promises — the parts that keep platforms alive.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the API-design rep. Design an API for a partner integration you know — real or simulated — on paper.
1. Start with consumers and use cases: who calls this API, what jobs are they doing — consumers before endpoints.
2. Sketch the resources and methods: name the resources, the verbs, and the status-code vocabulary — REST literacy in practice.
3. Weigh the design tradeoffs: granularity, consistency, evolvability — and write down who pays for each choice.
4. Write the versioning and compatibility promise: what can change, what cannot, how deprecation works — the contract developers build on.
5. Choose webhooks versus polling for the event story: match to latency needs and consumer capability — and justify the choice in writing.
6. Design the boring parts: auth, rate limits, error shapes, idempotency — the contract work that keeps platforms alive.
7. Audit the DX: docs, SDKs, errors, onboarding — would a developer adopt this? Write the three friction points you would fix first.
8. Present the design aloud in ten minutes: consumers, tradeoffs, contract, DX — as you would in the API design round.

modules.title: Data Literacy for PMs
modules.summary: Welcome back to the Technical PM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 3: Data Literacy for PMs. Technical PMs live in data: querying it, instrumenting it, and knowing when it misleads. This module builds hands-on literacy with the tools analysts actually use. By the end of this module you will write the SQL a PM actually needs, design event instrumentation and taxonomies, read funnels and cohorts, build dashboards that answer questions, stay data-informed rather than data-driven, spot lying data, and work with data teams effectively.
objectives: Understand and apply: SQL literacy: joins, aggregations, windows
Understand and apply: event instrumentation and taxonomies
Understand and apply: funnels and cohort analysis
Understand and apply: dashboards that answer questions

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **SQL literacy (PM)** — Joins, aggregations, window functions — enough to answer your own questions without waiting in the analytics queue.
- **Event instrumentation** — Defining the events and properties the product emits — the data foundation; garbage taxonomy, garbage analysis.
- **Taxonomy** — The naming contract for events and properties: consistent, documented, versioned — the difference between analysis and archaeology.
- **Funnels and cohorts** — Funnels: where users drop. Cohorts: how behavior differs by group and over time — the PM's diagnostic pair.
- **Decision dashboards** — Designed around decisions, not data availability — every chart should imply an action.
- **Data-informed versus data-driven** — Informed: data inputs to judgment. Driven: judgment abdicated to data — know which you are doing.
- **Lying data** — Instrumentation bugs, selection bias, Simpson's paradox, vanity metrics — skepticism is a data skill.
- **Working with data teams** — Clear questions, shared definitions, realistic timelines — the partnership that keeps analysis trustworthy.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the data-literacy rep set. Use a product you know — real or simulated — and work the data by hand.
1. Write three SQL queries a PM actually needs: a join across two tables, an aggregation by day, and a window function ranking users — answer your own question.
2. Design the event taxonomy for one user flow: the events, the properties, the naming contract — garbage taxonomy means garbage analysis.
3. Sketch the funnel for that flow and a cohort comparison: where users drop, how behavior differs by group — the diagnostic pair.
4. Design a decision dashboard: three charts maximum, each implying an action — designed around decisions, not data availability.
5. Write the data-informed decision memo: the data, your judgment, and which one carried the decision — know which you are doing.
6. Play skeptic: invent three ways your own dashboard could be lying — instrumentation bug, selection bias, Simpson's paradox — and how you would check each.
7. Write the data-team request: the question, the definitions, the timeline — the partnership brief that gets good analysis back.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **LLMs at product altitude** — Next-token prediction over learned patterns: fluent, probabilistic, knowledge-cutoff-bound — enough to reason about product fit.
- **Tokens** — The model's unit of text and of billing: count them — they are money.
- **Context window** — The model's finite working memory: what fits, what gets truncated, and what it costs to fill.
- **Capabilities** — What models do well: drafting, summarizing, transforming, conversing within distribution — fluency tasks with verifiable outputs.
- **Limits** — Hallucination, weak reasoning on novel problems, knowledge cutoffs — the boundaries every AI PM must design around.
- **Latency basics** — Time-to-first-token versus total time; model size versus quality — the arithmetic of AI user experience.
- **Model selection** — When the flagship is overkill: match capability to the task with evals, not hype.
- **Hype filter** — Demos versus products: the demo shows the best case; the product survives the worst case.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the GenAI literacy drill. Work each step on paper — the arithmetic is the literacy.
1. Write the product-altitude mental model in your own words: probabilistic next-token prediction, cutoff-bound — and what that implies for product fit.
2. Price a feature: pick a task (e.g. summarizing 50 tickets a day), estimate tokens in and out, and compute the monthly cost at a stated per-token price — tokens are money.
3. Fill a context window on paper: list what must fit (instructions, examples, retrieved docs, the task) and what gets truncated first — the finite working memory, managed.
4. List three capabilities and three limits for a feature you would ship: where the model is fluent and verifiable, and where hallucination or cutoffs would bite.
5. Weigh the latency tradeoff: time-to-first-token versus total, streaming versus batch — and write the UX consequence of each.
6. Run the model-selection test: would a smaller model pass your evals for this task? Write the criteria that would prove it — match capability to task, not hype.
7. Apply the hype filter to a demo you have seen: what was the best case shown, and what would the worst case cost the product?

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Chat pattern** — The default pattern — and its trap: defaulting to chat for everything, where many tasks need structured UI, not conversation.
- **Copilots** — AI inside existing workflows: suggest, complete, accelerate — the user stays in control.
- **Agents** — When the model takes actions: multi-step tasks with tool use where autonomy pays — and where the failure modes are acceptable.
- **RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)** — Grounding answers in your data with citations — for knowledge tasks where freshness and verifiability matter.

modules.summary: Welcome back to the GenAI track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 3: Evaluation and UX for AI. AI products are probabilistic, so their UX and evaluation must be designed for uncertainty: evals that catch regressions, interfaces that communicate confidence, and the discipline to not ship AI where determinism is required. By the end of this module you will design evals with golden datasets and calibrated judges, build human feedback loops, design UX for uncertainty, build trust through transparency, mitigate failure modes in the interface, run the eval-ship-measure loop, and know when not to use AI at all.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:

- **Golden dataset** — Representative real cases with known-good answers — the ground truth your evals measure against.
- **Human feedback loops** — Corrections and ratings that improve the system over time — usage funding evaluation.
- **UX for uncertainty** — Confidence display, sources, undo, corrections — honest interfaces for probabilistic outputs.
- **Trust and transparency** — Show what the AI did and why, cite sources, admit limits — trust is designed, not assumed.
- **Failure-mode UX mitigations** — Each known failure gets an interface answer: fallback, escalation, or graceful refusal — designed, not discovered.
- **Iteration loop** — Eval, ship, measure — the cadence that keeps AI features improving after launch.
- **The no-AI decision** — The discipline to not ship AI where determinism is required or errors are catastrophic.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run the eval-and-UX drill on an AI feature you would ship — real or simulated.

3. Design the human feedback loop: what corrections and ratings the product collects, and how they flow back into the system — usage funding evaluation.
4. Sketch the UX for uncertainty: confidence display, sources, undo, corrections — the honest interface for probabilistic outputs.
5. List the feature's three most likely failure modes and write the interface answer for each: fallback, escalation, or graceful refusal — designed, not discovered.
6. Write the transparency spec: what the AI did, why, its sources, its admitted limits — trust designed, not assumed.
7. Run the no-AI test: is determinism required here, or are errors catastrophic? If yes, write the non-AI alternative — the discipline to say no.

    ('u1', 'pro', 'signup'), ('u1', 'pro', 'activate'), ('u1', 'pro', 'purchase'),
    ('u2', 'free', 'signup'), ('u2', 'free', 'activate'),
    ('u3', 'pro', 'signup'),
    ('u4', 'free', 'signup'), ('u4', 'free', 'activate'), ('u4', 'free', 'purchase'),
    ('u5', 'free', 'signup'),
], columns=['user', 'plan', 'event'])
steps = ['signup', 'activate', 'purchase']

# TODO: for each plan, compute users reaching each step and step-to-step conversion.
# Print a funnel table and name the worst drop-off step per plan.
scriptLabs.hint: Pivot users x steps into a boolean matrix (crosstab), then cumsum across steps can't decrease — use cumulative reach per step and divide successive steps.
scriptLabs.solution:
import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame([
    ('u1', 'pro', 'signup'), ('u1', 'pro', 'activate'), ('u1', 'pro', 'purchase'),
    ('u2', 'free', 'signup'), ('u2', 'free', 'activate'),
    ('u3', 'pro', 'signup'),
    ('u4', 'free', 'signup'), ('u4', 'free', 'activate'), ('u4', 'free', 'purchase'),
    ('u5', 'free', 'signup'),
], columns=['user', 'plan', 'event'])
steps = ['signup', 'activate', 'purchase']

reach = (events.assign(hit=1).pivot_table(index=['plan', 'user'], columns='event',
                                           values='hit', fill_value=0))
# a user 'reaches' a step only if they completed all prior steps
for i, s in enumerate(steps):
    prior = steps[:i + 1]
    reach[s + '_reached'] = (reach[prior].sum(axis=1) == len(prior)).astype(int)

funnel = reach.groupby('plan')[[s + '_reached' for s in steps]].sum()
print('--- funnel: users reaching each step ---')
print(funnel)
print('--- step conversion ---')
conv = funnel.copy()
for i in range(1, len(steps)):
    conv[steps[i]] = funnel[steps[i] + '_reached'] / funnel[steps[i - 1] + '_reached']
print(conv[steps[1:]].round(2))
worst = (1 - conv[steps[1:]]).idxmax(axis=1)
print('worst drop-off step per plan:')
print(worst)

scriptLabs.hint: Pooled p = (conv_a+conv_b)/(n_a+n_b); SE = sqrt(p(1-p)(1/n_a+1/n_b)); z = (rate_b-rate_a)/SE; two-sided p via math.erf.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math

def ab_test(conv_a, n_a, conv_b, n_b, alpha=0.05):
    ra, rb = conv_a / n_a, conv_b / n_b
    lift = (rb - ra) / ra
    p_pool = (conv_a + conv_b) / (n_a + n_b)
    se = math.sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1 / n_a + 1 / n_b))
    z = (rb - ra) / se
    p = 2 * (1 - 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))))
    verdict = 'significant' if p < alpha else 'not significant'
    print(f'A: {ra:.3%}  B: {rb:.3%}  lift: {lift:+.1%}  z={z:.2f}  p={p:.4f} -> {verdict} at alpha={alpha}')
    return {'rate_a': ra, 'rate_b': rb, 'lift': lift, 'z': z, 'p': p}

ab_test(120, 4000, 150, 4000)
print('Pitfalls to state in the interview: peeking inflates false positives; '
      'significance is not importance (check the absolute lift); '
      'segment before celebrating.')

scenarios.title: Leading through an incident
scenarios.context: You are the EM on call. Checkout is down, the war room has 14 people, two teams blame each other’s deploy, and the CEO is asking for an ETA in the channel.

options.text: Assign blame, then debug
options.why: Blame freezes the room — the incident needs mitigation first, attribution later in the postmortem.

options.text: Declare yourself incident commander, split the room into mitigation and comms, set a 15-minute update cadence
options.why: The EM scenario reps teach: take command, parallelize mitigation vs communication, and make status predictable — ETA pressure gets a cadence, not a guess.

options.text: Stay quiet and let the loudest engineer drive
options.why: Abdication is not leadership — the room needs structure, and that is the EM’s job.

steps.prompt: The CEO wants a root cause in 10 minutes. You respond?

options.text: Give the most likely cause as fact
options.why: Premature certainty becomes the official story and misdirects the fix — managing up means honest uncertainty.

options.text: ‘Mitigation is underway; we’ll confirm root cause before stating it — next update in 15 minutes’
options.why: Managing up on delivery risk: acknowledge, bound the uncertainty, commit to the cadence — trust is built on reliable updates, not fast guesses.

options.text: Ignore the CEO until it’s fixed
options.why: Silence breeds escalation — proactive comms keep leadership aligned while you work.

steps.prompt: After mitigation, what makes the postmortem change behavior?

options.text: A detailed timeline only
options.why: Timelines record; action items with owners and dates change — the retrospective must produce both.

options.text: Blameless timeline, root causes, action items with owners and due dates, and a follow-up review
options.why: The module’s rule: retrospectives that change behavior have owners, dates, and a revisit — otherwise they are theater.

options.text: A private note to the engineer who shipped the bug
options.why: Individual blame teaches hiding; systemic fixes teach learning.

options.text: Start a PIP immediately
options.why: A PIP without documented feedback and support is both unfair and legally fragile — process starts with clarity, not punishment.

options.text: Private, specific feedback: observed impact, expectations, support offered — documented
options.why: The people-leadership module: feedback that lands is private, behavioral, impact-linked, and paired with support — documented from the start.

options.text: Reassign their work quietly and hope
options.why: Quiet workarounds punish the team and teach the senior nothing — avoidance compounds the problem.

steps.prompt: They improve for a month, then regress. Now?

options.text: Give up — some people can’t change
options.why: One cycle is not a verdict; but the pattern now needs formal structure.

options.text: A formal performance plan: clear bar, timeline, check-ins, consequences — with HR partnership
options.why: Performance management escalates fairly: explicit expectations, support, timeline, and honest consequences — the module’s PIP discipline.

options.text: Extend informal feedback another two quarters

scenarios.title: The AI feature launch decision

options.text: Launch — 88% is good enough
options.why: Unsupported claims in a summarizer are a trust defect at scale — shipping known hallucinations is a product decision with owners, and the owner would be you.

options.text: Delay the auto-publish; ship with citations, confidence display, and human review for low-confidence outputs — plus the eval gate for full launch
options.why: The GenAI PM playbook: UX for uncertainty (confidence, sources, undo), evals as the launch gate, and the discipline to not ship AI where the failure mode is unacceptable.

options.text: Cancel the feature entirely
options.why: One measured failure mode with mitigations available is not a cancellation — it is a scoped launch.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a program you turned around.
answerBank.a: Structure: the red signals I found (missed milestones, unowned dependencies), how I re-scoped with explicit exit criteria, the dependency map I rebuilt across teams, the risk register with mitigations and owners, and the comms cadence that restored trust. Close with the outcome and what the turnaround taught me about early warning signs — interviewers score structured thinking and honest ownership, so I name what I got wrong first.

answerBank.q: How do you influence without authority?
answerBank.a: I build a stakeholder map, run decisions through written logs so nothing is tribal, escalate crisply with options instead of problems, and follow through relentlessly — trust compounds. When teams conflict, I reframe around the shared outcome and make the tradeoff explicit. My example: aligning two EMs and a PM on a platform migration by getting the dependency risks and the rollback plan agreed in writing before anyone committed dates.

Private, specific, documented feedback first: observed behaviors, business impact, clear expectations, and the support I’ll provide — with a check-in date. If the pattern continues, a formal plan with HR: explicit bar, timeline, and consequences. I’ve learned to start these conversations earlier than feels comfortable, because delay is unfair to the rest of the team. I can walk through a real case: what I tried, where I misread the situation, and what changed.

answerBank.q: How do you decide what to build? (product sense)
answerBank.a: I start from the user and the problem: who hurts, how often, what they do today — asking why until I hit the real need. Then I frame the market, size the opportunity, and prioritize by impact versus effort with my assumptions stated out loud so they can be challenged. I’d demonstrate with a teardown: what a product gets right, where it fails users, and what I’d change first — critiquing by mechanism, not taste.

answerBank.q: A key metric dropped 15% yesterday. Walk me through it.
answerBank.a: Before reacting, I debug: is the instrumentation intact, which segments moved, is it a real behavior change or a reporting artifact, and what shipped or happened externally in the window. I’d check funnels and cohorts to localize, look for confounders like seasonality or a partial rollout, and only then form hypotheses — ranked by likelihood — with the test that would confirm each. The discipline is: understand the move before acting on it.

answerBank.q: How do you evaluate a technical tradeoff as a PM? (build vs buy)
answerBank.a: I frame it as total cost of ownership: build cost plus maintenance, hiring, and opportunity cost versus buy cost plus integration, lock-in, and roadmap dependence. I check which parts are differentiating IP — build those — versus commodity — buy those. Then I pressure-test with engineering on reliability and scale assumptions, and I write the decision with its tradeoffs so it survives personnel changes. I’d give a real example with the numbers I used.

answerBank.q: Should we ship this AI feature? The demo is great but evals are shaky.
answerBank.a: The demo doesn’t decide — the evals do. I’d quantify the failure modes: rate, severity, and who gets hurt, then check whether UX mitigations (citations, confidence display, human review on low-confidence outputs) bound the risk acceptably for a scoped launch. If not, we delay with a clear eval gate for launch and a kill criterion. I’d bring executives a pre-read: the numbers, the business risk, the mitigated plan — because shipping known AI failures is a product decision with an owner, and I’d rather own the delay than the incident.

terminalSims.brief: Practice the leadership scenario-round command set — brief, clarify, options, decide, debrief — against a realistic canned sandbox.

commands.out:
Usage: lead <command> [options]

Commands:
  brief    Show the current scenario brief
  clarify  List the clarifying questions to ask first
  options  Lay out options with tradeoffs
  decide   Record a decision with rationale
  debrief  Review the decision afterward

SCENARIO 7 — 'The slipping quarter':
Your team is 3 weeks behind on a committed launch with 4 weeks left.
The VP asks for a plan by tomorrow. Structure: clarify, options, tradeoffs, decision.

Clarifying questions:
  1. What exactly is committed — scope, date, or both?
  2. What caused the slip — scope creep, estimation, dependency?
  3. What are the fixed constraints — headcount, dependencies, quality bar?

Options:
  A. Cut scope — ship the core, defer the rest. Tradeoff: smaller launch.
  B. Add people — Tradeoff: onboarding cost, Brooks's law risk.
  C. Move the date — Tradeoff: credibility cost, stakeholder impact.
  D. Cut quality — Tradeoff: tech debt and incident risk. (Not recommended.)

commands.cmd: lead decide --option A --rationale "Protect the date and quality; defer scope with stakeholder agreement"
commands.out:
Decision recorded: Option A.
Rationale: Protect the date and quality; defer scope with stakeholder agreement.
Rubric: clarify ✓, options ✓, tradeoffs ✓, decision ✓.

Debrief prompts:
  - What did you decide, and what did you miss?
  - What would you change with one more hour?
  - Which tradeoff was hardest to defend?

terminalSims.brief: Run Fermi-style estimation drills — assumptions first, round-number math, sanity-check the answer. The reasoning chain is the grade.

commands.out:
Usage: est <command>

Commands:
  start        Begin a new estimation drill
  assumptions  State your assumptions aloud
  math         Show the round-number math
  check        Sanity-check the answer

DRILL 12: How many engineering managers does a 5,000-person tech company need?
State assumptions first. Round numbers only.

Assumptions (yours to state; example):
  - ~60% of 5,000 are in engineering ≈ 3,000
  - Span of control ≈ 7 engineers per manager
  - ~15% overhead for senior/skip-level managers

Math:
  3,000 engineers ÷ 7 per manager ≈ 430 team managers
  +15% overhead ≈ 495 → round to ~500 managers.

Sanity check:
  - 500 managers / 5,000 staff = 10% — plausible for a tech org.
  - If span were 5: ~690. If 10: ~345. Range 350–700 brackets the answer.
  Grade: chain stated, math round, sanity checked ✓
